transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jason Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Lena Morales (Aegis CTO), Samir Gupta (Aegis ML Eng), Priya Nair (Aegis Head of Product)

Auto-generated summary: (may be imperfect)
- Focus on pricing and unit economics, questions about batching, KV cache, prefix caching, and how Redwood's per-token maps to cost for their use-case.
- Action items: send pricing spreadsheet, schedule POC benchmark, customer to share token volumes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jason: Hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Jason from Redwood, i'm the AE on this, um with me is Maya who's our SE, she'll do the deep dive.. hows everyone doing?
[00:05] Lena: good thanks, busy day but excited to get this, thanks for squeezing us in.
[00:10] Priya: Hi. we wanted to focus mostly on cost because we have a tight monthly budget for inference.
[00:15] Jason: totally, today we'll go through hosted vs dedicated vs private and then show rough unit economics and levers like batching and caching that change cost per token.
[00:22] Maya: quick note, our numbers sometimes include token and model inference cost plus infra overhead; i'll show an example calc and also show where quantization and batching reduce costs.
[00:30] Samir: cool. to start, current stack: we're running a mix of open LLMs in-house and some calls to managed APIs, roughly 10M tokens/mo now, expected to 50M in 6 months, mostly short prompts (avg 60 tokens prompt, 80 tokens response) and some long chat sessions ~800 tokens.
[00:48] Jason: that volume's helpful. what's the primary SLO? are you optimizing for latency or cost?
[00:52] Lena: latency matters for chat features, we want sub-300ms token latency in interactive flows, but for batch scoring nightly we can tolerate higher latency. budget is a hard constraint though - we're allocated ~$12k/mo for inference right now.
[01:04] Maya: ok that helps. hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value and per-token billing, Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and lower unit cost at scale, Private (VPC/on-prem) solves for data residency and stricter security but higher ops overhead.
[01:18] Samir: can you give numbers? rough per-token figures so we can model it.
[01:22] Jason: sure i'll share the spreadsheet after, but roughly for our curated open model family: Hosted list price around $0.0035 per 1k tokens for generation for model X (example), embeddings different. Dedicated committed pricing can drop that to ~$0.0012 per 1k tokens depending on commit and batching. these are illustrative numbers.
[01:39] Priya: sorry, is that per 1k input+output tokens or just output?
[01:43] Maya: typically per-token covers both input+output. we'll make that explicit in the spreadsheet. also there are infra egress and other optional charges for private deployments.
[01:50] Lena: how does batching affect the per-token cost? we do a lot of short requests, so single-request cost seems high.
[01:56] Maya: good question. batching aggregates multiple prompts into one generation call on the GPU to improve GPU utilization, so you amortize kernel overhead. for throughput-oriented workloads batching can reduce cost per token by 20-60% depending on batch size and sequence length. for interactive low-latency chat, continuous batching with small windows (10-30ms) can still give benefit without killing latency.
[02:20] Samir: what's continuous batching?
[02:22] Maya: it's where the runtime holds requests for a small time-slice to collect other requests and form a batch. it's a tradeoff of a few ms additional latency vs better utilization. we expose policies to control that.
[02:31] Jason: also our caching layers matter: prefix caching and KV cache for long conversations can prevent re-computing tokens. e.g., if you have repeated system prompts or embeddings cached, you save tokens and compute. that's especially helpful for chat where conversation context is repetitive across users.
[02:45] Priya: do you have examples?
[02:47] Maya: yes for one customer we saw effective token savings of ~35% from prefix caching plus short-term KV caching on 2-3 turn conversations, depends on prompt reuse.
[02:56] Samir: interesting. for our long sessions (~800 tokens) how does KV cache help?
[03:00] Maya: KV cache avoids recomputing the attention state for previous tokens in autoregressive decoding; when users scroll or continue sessions we only compute new tokens. it doesn't reduce the token count emitted but reduces GPU work for repeated contexts - but it's model/runtime dependent.
[03:12] Lena: okay. on dedicated, you mentioned reserved GPUs. if we commit to Dedicated, is there a way to automatically fallback to Hosted if we spike?
[03:19] Jason: yes we have smart routing and fallback tiers - you can pin primary to Dedicated and allow overflow to Hosted or cheaper model variants. that helps handle spikes without outages.
[03:28] Priya: for our budgeting, we need a predictable monthly cost. do dedicated committed plans offer predictable billing?
[03:34] Jason: Dedicated is typically a fixed monthly capacity fee (committed), which makes unit economics predictable; you can combine with burst/overflow to Hosted. we'll include scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[03:42] Samir: how sensitive are numbers to quantization? we use some 4-bit quantized models internally.
[03:46] Maya: quantization reduces model memory and can increase throughput; depending on hardware the throughput-to-cost improvement varies. in our internal tests, moving from fp16 to 4-bit can give 1.5-2x throughput gains for some models, which translates to lower $/token when CPU/GPU time is the dominant cost. we'll note model-specific guidance.
[04:05] [04:05] Lena: there's also security concerns - SOC2, audit logs, SSO. we will likely need SOC2 type 2 and SSO integration. what do you support?
[04:12] Jason: we support SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integrations for private deployments, audit logs in Redwood Console, and we have SOC 2 compliance documentation - i'll send those. for Dedicated and Private we can integrate with customer KMS or HSM.
[04:24] Priya: good. for private deployment is there a big price premium?
[04:27] Maya: Private has platform fee + support and typically higher ops cost. per-token compute might be similar if you're running equivalent GPUs, but the managed platform fee and initial setup are higher. we'll quote both TCO and $/token comparable numbers.
[04:38] Samir: when you say per-token pricing, does that include the savings from batching/caching or is it nominal?
[04:43] Maya: list per-token is nominal; effective $/token we show in the spreadsheet will include expected savings from typical batching/caching policies based on workload profiles. that's why we ask for sample prompt distributions - to give an expected effective unit price.
[04:55] Jason: maybe we can walk through a quick toy calc live: assume 50M tokens/mo, mostly short 60/80 split, hosted list price of $0.0035/1k tokens => that's about $175/mo? (note: math is approximate)
[05:08] Samir: wait that seems off, 50M tokens at $0.0035 per 1k tokens should be 50,000 * 0.0035 = $175. okay that is right. but then 50 million tokens isn't that high.. we need to ensure the per-token units align with our current spend expectations.
[05:20] Maya: right, but if you have a lot of small high-frequency requests the real cost is higher because overhead per request reduces batching. with better batching you could be lower. Dedicated committed pricing might cut that by ~2-3x.
[05:30] Priya: our current plan is $12k/mo; does Redwood have customer examples fitting that budget at 50M tokens?
[05:36] Jason: yes, some customers at that budget use Dedicated with commit or carefully tuned batching on Hosted. we'll model a few scenarios for you.
[05:43] Lena: when you model, please include an example that forces low-latency chat (sub-300ms) vs a throughput heavy batch scoring, because the achievable batching savings differ a lot.
[05:53] Maya: will do. also note that you can mix models - use faster cheaper quantized variants for lower criticality paths and use higher quality models for critical flows; routing policies can help minimize cost while preserving quality.
[06:05] Samir: sounds good. what's the typical time to run a POC benchmark? we want real numbers on our prompts.
[06:10] Jason: typical POC is 1-2 weeks: first week instrumenting and rehearsing sample dataset, second week run benchmark across scenarios. Maya will run the benchmark on Dedicated (if you want) or Hosted depending on availability.
[06:20] Maya: for benchmarking we ask for a token export (csv), sample prompts, and a defined SLA target. we'll simulate traffic patterns and provide $/token and latency distributions.
[06:28] Priya: Samir will send the token export and sample prompt set.
[06:31] Samir: yep, i'll get that by friday.
[06:33] Jason: thanks. quick deep dive on how we calculate effective $/token: we take raw compute cost (GPU hours * cost/hr) + platform overhead / total effective tokens served after caching/dup reduction and amortize across commit or per-request. we'll include sample calcs in the spreadsheet.
[06:48] [06:48] Priya: about burst capacity -- if we do Dedicated commit, how do you charge for overflow to Hosted? is it the hosted list price or some blended rate?
[06:55] Maya: overflow is typically billed at the hosted list rate; depending on contract we can negotiate blended overflow pricing. Dedicated also comes with configurable burst policies and alarms to avoid surprise spend.
[07:06] Samir: do you expose tracing or token-level cost breakdowns in the console?
[07:10] Jason: yes per-route and per-model dashboards with token-level cost breakdowns, traces and error logs. helps you identify hot prompts that are expensive.
[07:18] Lena: ok. our procurement asks for a vendor security questionnaire and an initial TCO estimate - can you provide those?
[07:24] Jason: yes will send security docs and a TCO template.
[07:26] Priya: do you have a case study for someone similar size?
[07:29] Jason: yes i can share a couple case studies; i'll include a short one about a SaaS company that cut $/token by 2x moving to Dedicated with batching and prefix caching.
[07:37] Samir: any gotchas with token accounting - sometimes we see tokens counted differently across vendors.
[07:42] Maya: that's a good point. tokenization differences (e.g., byte-pair vs other) affect the token counts; we try to standardize on tiktoken for comparisons, but we'll align with your tokenizer when we run the benchmark.
[07:53] Jason: wrapping up, agreed next steps: Jason to send pricing spreadsheet and security docs; Maya to book POC and run benchmarks; Samir to provide token export & prompts.
[08:05] Priya: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[08:07] Lena: thanks, we'll review the materials and aim to lock a POC by end of month.
[08:11] Jason: great, talk soon.
